prize_parts.citation: for analyses of how technology and international trade reshape labour demand, wage inequality and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: I keep B037 first after reading the openings. The discovery combines new data, transparent quasi-experimental designs (local labour-market exposure to import competition) and an explanatory framework (task-based and skill-biased accounts of labour demand). Together these explain who gains and loses from technological and trade change and why adjustment is slow and uneven. The work is general, concerns a big and hard question, and has changed research agendas and public policy debate. It is also old enough, roughly two decades for the framework and over a decade for the China-shock evidence, to have been replicated, extended and partly challenged, so its durable influence can be judged. This is a view on the scientific contribution only. Opening support counts are not evidence of merit, and I do not rely on them. Where others ranked B037 lower, I have tried to take their reasons seriously rather than treat the ranking as settled.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that B037 combines two strands with different credit structures: the task and skill-premium framework, and the import-competition evidence. A three-name cap cuts through both. Dorn is a co-author of the central China-shock papers and is excluded, while Katz's skill-premium work is partly entangled with the Goldin-Katz research already close to the 2023 prize. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the measurement of task change, are still debated. If the committee judges the two strands to be separate discoveries, this ballot is weaker than a cleanly attributable single discovery.

responses.point: Stromberg ranked B037 sixth. He sees overlap with the Goldin and Acemoglu prizes and a composite credit set, in which Katz is linked to Goldin and the task framework is partly Acemoglu's, so choosing three names means picking among overlapping lines.
responses.response: The credit problem is real, and I accept it as the main weakness. I weigh the overlap differently. The 2023 prize cited women's labour-market outcomes over time, and the 2024 prize cited institutions and prosperity. Neither cited the demand-side account of how technology and trade shocks reallocate labour and wages, or the local-labour-market designs that measure those effects. Related inputs from prior laureates do not make this discovery already recognised. The uncredited task-framework authors (Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane) do limit how much the citation can claim for the framework, so I would word it around the combined technology and trade-adjustment evidence. I would not word it as a claim to have originated the task model.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B037 first with Autor, Hanson and Katz. He also names Dorn's omission under the three-laureate cap as a real attribution cost, and notes that the tasks and trade-shock strands may be seen as separable contributions.
responses.response: I agree that dropping Dorn is a cost. Friberg's trio of Autor, Hanson and Dorn is a defensible alternative that covers the trade-shock strand more tightly. I still choose Katz because the committee would then credit both the labour-demand framework and the trade-shock evidence, and Autor connects them. I do not think this is clearly right. If colleagues judge the two strands separable, the cleaner trio is the trade-shock one, and I would want the committee to decide that on attribution grounds rather than by default.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B001 (Obstfeld and Rogoff) first because it has a compact two-name attribution, thoroughly confirmed contributions and is overdue. He ranks B037 second and calls its credit spread across several authors.
responses.response: A clean two-name attribution is a real advantage, and B037 does worse on it. Clean credit is not by itself scientific merit, though. I ranked B001 sixth because I see the exchange-rate disconnect puzzles as unresolved, so the empirical side of the discovery is an open problem rather than a confirmed result. My own field gives me less basis to second-guess the framework's theoretical importance, and I defer to the macroeconomists on that. I would still weigh B037's replicated, design-based evidence and its policy reach more heavily. Even so, B001 is a strong and legitimate competitor on the substance.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the technology (task and skill-premium) and import-competition strands as one discovery or as two.
Katz versus Dorn for the third place, and how much Katz's skill-premium work overlaps with Goldin's recognised research.
How persistent and how large the China-shock effects were, and how well task change is measured.
How credit should be assigned for the task framework to authors outside the credited names.
My comparative judgement on the macroeconomic candidates (B013, B001, B025) relies on colleagues' arguments, because they are outside my own research area.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My profile lists no co-authorship with any B037 credited person, and the coauthors it names are not on that ballot. I presented the 2023 prize (Goldin) at the announcement. That work is adjacent to Katz's earlier collaboration, but it is not a personal or institutional tie to him.
